items.equation: LHS drawdowns at t=0: principal €5000 + financed broker fee €200 = €5200 treated as a single t=0 drawdown (the fee inflates the amount the consumer is obliged to repay, so it sits on the drawdowns side of the equation, NOT on the repayments side as a t=0 fee). Repayments side: month-12 payment = 5200*(1+0.08) = 5616 (simple interest since nominal 8% with single payment). For the actuarial form: 5200 = 5616*(1+X)^-12.
items.iterations:
Solve (1+X)^12 = 5616/5200 = 1.08 → 1+X = 1.08^(1/12) = 1.006434 → X = 0.006434 (monthly rate).
  Direct check at X=0.006434: (1.006434)^12 = 1.0800 → 5200*1.0800 = 5616.00. PV: 5616*(1.006434)^-12 = 5616/1.08 = 5200. f=0.
  Iteration count for the solver: 1 (closed-form). For mechanical solvers shown: iter 1 X=0.005 → PV of 5616 at 0.005/12 = (1.005)^12*... Actually re-run: 5616*(1.005)^-12 = 5616/1.0617 = 5289.7 > 5200, f<0, LOWER X. Iter 2 X=0.007: 5616*(1.007)^-12 = 5616/1.0872 = 5166.0 < 5200, f>0. Iter 3 X=0.0064: 5616*(1.0064)^-12 = 5204.6, f>0. Convergence between 0.0064 and 0.007; true value 0.006434.
  Annual: effective APR = (1.006434)^12 - 1 = 8.00% (because the 8% nominal is itself a single-period-of-12-months rate; no compounding gain). Reported APRC = 8.0%.
  Note on financed fee: had the €200 been a t=0 CASH fee (not financed), the equation would be 5000 = 5616*(1+X)^-12 - 200 — but that violates PV balance unless we re-interpret: a cash fee at t=0 INCREASES the effective cost because the consumer pays €200 immediately PLUS repays the full €5200. The PV equation would be 5000 = 200 + 5200*(1+X)^-12 → X higher than 8%. The 'financed' treatment LOWERS the headline APRC vs. cash-paid fee because the fee gets amortised.

weakest_point: Case 2: the directive's Annex I overdraft assumptions (Part II §2 default 3-month duration, §3 instalment structure) are applied to a clean test case, but in real-world APRC computations the most common source of divergence between implementations is (a) whether the monthly €25 fee is placed on the REPAYMENTS side at its respective t_i (correct per Art. 17(2) and Annex I) or netted into the instalment by the calculator's internal amortisation, and (b) the periodicity convention — the directive requires solving for X as a rate per 'unit period' (here 1 month) and then stating it as an annual rate, but the conversion (multiply by 12 vs. (1+X)^12-1) differs across national transpositions. For this specific 3-month overdraft, the conversion only modestly affects the number (effective 30.5% vs nominal 26.9%), but a single national transposition could publish either. This is the highest-divergence risk in the set.

assumptions_invoked: Actuarial method: PV of drawdowns = PV of repayments+charges, discounted at monthly periods, then annualized via (1+i_month)^12 - 1

The €100 arrangement fee, paid at conclusion (t=0), is treated as DEDUCTED from the loan proceeds actually made available to the consumer — net amount drawn down used in the equation is €10,000 - €100 = €9,900, while the repayment schedule (24 × €450) remains based on the full €10,000 nominal principal
Repayments of €450 occur at t=1,2,...,24 months (ordinary annuity, first payment one month after drawdown, as stated)
items.iterations: Iter1: i=0.0060 -> annuity factor f(i)=(1-(1+i)^-24)/i = 22.286 (target factor = 9900/450 = 22.000, too high). Iter2: i=0.0070 -> f(i)=22.022 (still slightly high). Iter3: i=0.0072 -> f(i)=21.968 (now too low). Linear interpolation between iter2/iter3 gives i≈0.007082. Convergence check: f(0.007082)=22.001 ≈ 22.000 (residual 0.001, accepted). Converged monthly i≈0.7082%.

assumptions_invoked: Full €1,500 limit drawn immediately (stated in case)

Repayment structure of 12 equal monthly instalments is an assumed simplification for this worked case (source-logic: mirrors the directive's general fallback of assuming a plausible, fully-amortizing repayment schedule when the actual open-end repayment pattern is not otherwise specified) — this is NOT a specific numbered CCD Annex I assumption being cited, but a constructed convention for tractability
18% nominal per annum, monthly compounding = 1.5% monthly rate, applied uniformly to both the amortization schedule and the discounting rate
No fees or charges other than interest, so the equal instalment is exactly the standard amortizing-loan payment at the same rate used for discounting
items.equation: 1500 = A * [1-(1.015)^-12]/0.015, where A is solved as the standard annuity payment: A = 1500*0.015/[1-(1.015)^-12] = 137.52; since drawdown and repayment side are both built from i=0.015 by construction, APRC = (1.015)^12 - 1 directly
items.iterations: No iterative root-finding required: because the instalment amount A was derived directly from the stated 1.5%-monthly rate as a standard amortization formula, the PV equation is satisfied exactly at i=0.015 by construction (closed-form; residual = 0 by definition). Convergence check: substituting i=0.015 back into the PV equation reproduces 1500 exactly (verified algebraically, not iteratively).

assumptions_invoked: Full €5,000 limit drawn down at t=0, assumed because the case specifies an 'unascertainable drawdown timing/pattern,' and the directive's general fallback in such cases is to assume the maximum/full amount is drawn immediately (a conservative, fully-drawn assumption analogous to the overdraft full-drawdown convention)

Rate of 8% nominal per annum applied as simple annual compounding over the single 12-month period (since there is only one compounding interval between drawdown and the single repayment, nominal annual and effective annual coincide here)

The €200 broker fee is FINANCED into the balance: it is added to the outstanding principal (5000+200=5200) at t=0 and therefore itself accrues interest at 8% for the year, but it is NOT part of the amount actually made available to the consumer for their own use — so the 'amount of credit' on the drawdown side of the APRC equation remains €5,000, while the repayment side is based on the grown 5200 balance
items.iterations: No iterative solving required: single drawdown / single repayment pair gives a closed-form solution. (1+X) = 5616/5000 = 1.1232, so X = 0.1232. Convergence check: substituting X=0.1232 back gives 5616/1.1232 = 5000.0 exactly (verified algebraically).

weakest_point: The single largest source of potential divergence from the directive's exact prescribed method is the fee-treatment convention chosen in cases 1 and 4 (whether an upfront/financed fee reduces the net drawdown, is added to the repayment stream, or is added to the accruing principal) — the CCD Annex I text is prescriptive about which convention applies to which fee type, and this computation applied a self-consistent but explicitly-chosen convention rather than one confirmed against the annex's literal fee-classification rules. Secondary risk: case 2's fee-timing assumption (fees paid at month-end, interest compounding monthly rather than simple) and its use of a 3-month duration (as instructed, not the directive's own general 1-year default) are both assumptions of convenience rather than verified annex-mandated treatments.

trailing_objects.financed_vs_cash_fee_note: Contrast for case 4: a financed fee is added to the principal balance and therefore compounds at the credit's own interest rate for the full period before being repaid, inflating the total repayment (5200*1.08=5616) while leaving the discounted drawdown side unchanged at 5000. A t=0 CASH fee instead reduces the net amount actually drawn down (e.g. 5000-200=4800) while the repayment obligation is computed on the original undiminished principal (5000*1.08=5400) — giving a different equation (4800 = 5400*(1+X)^-1, X=0.125=12.5%) and a different APRC (12.5% vs 12.3%) even though the fee amount and nominal rate are identical, because in the financed case the fee itself earns interest for the period whereas in the cash case it does not.

items.financed_fee_note: A t=0 cash fee reduces the net amount made available to the consumer (net drawdown = principal - fee), leaving the repayment stream unchanged - it raises the APRC because the consumer receives less up front. A fee financed into the balance instead increases the drawn amount (drawdown rises from €5,000 to €5,200) while the repayment is calculated on that larger balance; here the repayment is 8% of €5,200, so the APRC remains exactly 8% - the fee is silently amortised into the loan rather than paid out of pocket.
